title: The Supreme Court Is About to Decide If H-1B Children Born in America Are Citizens
excerpt: Trump v. Barbara could reshape the 14th Amendment for the first time in 128 years. More than 300,000 Indian workers in the green card backlog are watching.
body:
The United States Supreme Court is expected to hand down its ruling in *Trump v. Barbara* within the next three weeks — a decision that could fundamentally alter the citizenship status of children born in America to parents on temporary visas. For the more than 300,000 Indian skilled workers waiting in the country's green card backlog, the stakes could not be higher.

The case centres on Executive Order 14160, signed by Trump on his first day back in office, which seeks to deny automatic birthright citizenship to children born in the U.S. if neither parent is a citizen or lawful permanent resident. It is the most direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause since its ratification in 1868.

## What Happened in Court

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on April 1, 2026, in a session that made history: Trump became the first sitting president to attend an oral argument, sitting in the front row for 90 minutes.

What he heard was not encouraging for his position. Six of the nine justices — including two he had appointed — pushed back sharply against the government's argument. Chief Justice John Roberts told the administration's lawyer: "It is a new world, but it is the same Constitution."

The government's position rested on a narrow reading of the 14th Amendment's phrase "subject to the jurisdiction thereof," arguing that children of temporary visa holders are not fully subject to U.S. jurisdiction. Legal scholars overwhelmingly reject this interpretation, pointing to the 1898 Supreme Court decision in *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, which held that the 14th Amendment grants citizenship to virtually all persons born on American soil.

The government notably declined to ask the court to overturn *Wong Kim Ark* — a signal that even the administration recognises the precedent's strength.

## The Indian Diaspora at the Centre

No community stands to be affected more directly than Indian Americans on temporary work visas. Three-quarters of all H-1B workers approved in recent fiscal years were born in India, according to Pew Research Center data. The per-country cap on employment-based green cards means that many Indian workers face wait times of decades — sometimes longer than their careers.

During that wait, their children are born in the United States. Under current law, those children are American citizens from their first breath. Under the executive order, they would not be — leaving them in a legal grey zone, eligible only for dependent visas tied to their parents' temporary status.

The American Immigration Lawyers Association has warned this would create "an underclass of children born in the U.S. who would never obtain citizenship." If a parent's green card never comes — a realistic possibility for many Indians in the backlog — neither would the child's pathway to permanent status.

## What a Ruling Could Look Like

Based on the oral arguments, most legal analysts expect the court to strike down the executive order, possibly by a 6-3 or larger margin. But the specific reasoning will matter enormously.

A narrow ruling could simply say the president lacks the power to redefine citizenship by executive order, leaving the door open for Congress to act legislatively. A broader ruling could reinforce *Wong Kim Ark* as settled law and foreclose future attempts to limit birthright citizenship without a constitutional amendment.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor raised the spectre of stateless newborns — children born in America who would have no citizenship anywhere. The scenario is not hypothetical for Indian families whose children would have no claim to Indian citizenship either, since India does not grant citizenship by descent to children born abroad unless registered with an Indian consulate.

## Trump Is Already Reacting

The president appears to be anticipating a loss. In a social media post in mid-May, he wrote: "They will be ruling against us on Birthright Citizenship, making us the only Country in the World that practices this unsustainable, unsafe, and incredibly costly DISASTER."

He added: "I don't want loyalty, but I do want and expect it for our Country."

The rhetoric echoes his reaction to the February tariff ruling, when Trump called the justices who voted against him "an embarrassment to their families." CNN reported that 23 cases remain pending, with birthright citizenship, executive power, and immigration protections all expected before the end of June.

## What H-1B Families Should Know

Immigration attorneys advise that current law remains unchanged while the case is pending. All children born in the United States today are citizens under the 14th Amendment. Federal court injunctions issued earlier in the litigation — including in *Barbara v. Trump* — remain in effect and protect families whose children have already been born.

The ruling is expected by late June or early July 2026.

For the Indian diaspora, it is a reminder that the most fundamental question — whether your American-born child is American — is now, for the first time in over a century, genuinely in play.

*Sources: CNN, Reuters, Knoxville News Sentinel, Bloomberg Law, American Immigration Lawyers Association, Pew Research Center*
